title: Learning disorders (dyslexia and dyscalculia)
intro: Specific learning disorders are lasting difficulties in learning to read, spell or do arithmetic that cannot be explained by low intelligence or poor teaching. Dyslexia affects reading and spelling, and dyscalculia affects numbers and calculation. With early recognition and tailored support, children can make good progress and build confidence.

sections.heading: What they are
paragraphs: Dyslexia involves problems connecting letters with sounds, reading fluently and spelling. Dyscalculia causes trouble understanding number concepts, memorising number facts and carrying out calculations. These disorders often run in families and are thought to involve differences in how the brain processes language and numbers.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: In dyslexia, a child may be slow to learn letters, confuse similar letters, read haltingly, avoid reading aloud or spell the same word differently. In dyscalculia, children may count on fingers long after peers, struggle with time and money or find maths homework overwhelming. Children may also develop low self-esteem, headaches or reluctance to attend school.

sections.heading: Assessment
paragraphs: Assessment is done by educational or clinical psychologists, paediatricians or specialist services, often together with the school. It includes tests of reading, spelling, maths and general abilities, and checks hearing, vision and other possible causes, such as attention problems or emotional stress, which may co-occur.

sections.heading: Support and teaching
paragraphs: Structured teaching that focuses on sound-letter links, reading practice and spelling or on number sense and calculation strategies is most helpful. Small steps, repeated practice, visual aids and encouragement support progress. Schools may offer extra time in tests, quiet space or the use of computers and spell checkers.
Strong subjects and interests should be nurtured, because success builds confidence. Regular practice in short sessions is better than long, tiring ones.

sections.heading: Parents and teachers
paragraphs: Praise effort and avoid comparisons. Stay in contact with teachers and ask about specific support plans. Some countries offer legal rights to accommodation and funding. Adults with these difficulties can also receive help at work and in further education.

examples.title: Starting a conversation
examples.text: Imagine your child avoids reading aloud and says they are stupid. You could meet the teacher, share what you notice at home and ask about screening and extra support.

examples.title: Supporting homework
examples.text: Suppose maths homework causes tears every evening. You might agree with the teacher on a shorter task, use objects or drawings to explain numbers, and take breaks.
